PRESCHOOL · AGE 3 · CLASS 4

Colors & Color Mixing

Age 3 YearsClass Preschool 4Subjects Colors & color mixing

Twenty-four cards in twelve color pairs, a rainbow to explore and printable sheets to solve at the table — this class follows Shapes & Patterns on the preschool path. Red, blue and yellow are old friends by now; today they learn to mix.

These mixing results are paint colors — the kind you get with real paints at the craft table. Start with the two colors your child already names best, and let the rest of the set wait its turn.

Start Today’s Class ↓Grown-up nearby, little one on the lap or wandering the room — both work.
TODAY’S CLASS

How today’s class works.

Five little steps, in any order that suits you: a welcome from your teacher, the color cards, the rainbow, solving the color sheets together, an off-screen hunt, and a warm goodbye. Stop after any step — that is a complete class, and there is never a score at the end.

  1. 1 Teacher welcome
  2. 2 Learn colors
  3. 3 Rainbow activity
  4. 4 Solve the sheets
  5. 5 Take it off screen
  6. 6 Class complete
TEACHER WELCOME

“Hello, my friend — and hello to you, grown-up helper! Today we’re playing with colors. We’ll look at splashes and name what we see — red like a strawberry, blue like the sky. Start with the colors your child already loves.”

— Your Kiddo School teacher

Begin the class ↓First stop: the color cards.
LEARN COLORS

Eleven splashes, eleven pictures, one rainbow.

First the pure color — a big, unmissable splash with its name. Then the same color living on a real thing: a red apple, a blue car, a gray elephant. Use the arrows to wander, or simply scroll. Name each color, then let your child spot it in the room before moving on.

Card 1 of 24
Or simply scroll: all 24 cards are below.
RAINBOW ACTIVITY

Every color at once.

The rainbow is the whole class in one arc: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple — in that famous order. Point at each stripe together and say its color, then tap the stripes below to check them off.

  1. 1red✓
  2. 2orange✓
  3. 3yellow✓
  4. 4green✓
  5. 5blue✓
  6. 6purple✓

Rainbow spotting

  • After rain, look for the real thing — sun plus shower makes rainbows, and one in the sky is a whole lesson.
  • No rainbow outside? Draw one together: six crayons, six arcs, any size of paper. A rainbow from memory counts.
SOLVE THE SHEETS — ON PAPER OR ON SCREEN

Solve the color sheets together.

The twelve color cards print two to a page — each color as a paint splash beside its matching picture. Printed, cut and named, they are the class’s real worksheets — and on screen, every card page can be drawn on directly.

  1. 01

    Print the cards

    Open the printable cards and print all twelve pairs, two to a page. Cut them out together, naming each color as it is cut.

  2. 02

    Name the splash

    Hold up a splash and name its color, then check the picture twin — red like a strawberry, yellow like a sun. Picture to color, color to picture.

  3. 03

    Sort the piles

    Sort the cards into little piles by color, then line them up rainbow-style: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple.

  4. 04

    Color the pictures

    On the picture cards, color the real twin with its crayon — the red strawberry gets red. On screen, the card page’s Write & Color layer is the crayon.

Open the printable cards ↗Draw on the cards on screen ↗

Every card page has a Write & Color layer: your child can draw right on the card with a finger, a stylus or the mouse, then save the finished work. Nothing is uploaded anywhere.

TAKE IT OFF SCREEN

Colors that live in your house.

Color words stick away from the screen, in short playful hunts with real things. Pick one of these — two minutes is plenty — and follow your child’s lead.

The color of the day

  • Pick one color card in the morning and hunt that color all day: clothes, cups, cars, cushions.
  • Keep a running count out loud — “that’s four red things!” — and let your child shout each new find.

Real paint mixing

  • Two blobs of washable, child-safe paint on paper — red and yellow first. Let your child swirl them with a brush or a finger and watch orange arrive.
  • Then blue + yellow, then red + blue. Grown-up job: stay close, protect the table, and let your child do ALL the stirring. No wiping mid-mix — the brown surprise can wait for another day.

Color snack plate

  • Snack time becomes color time: red strawberries, yellow banana, green cucumber, orange segments — name each color as you serve it.
  • Let your child build a plate of one single color for their teddy. Appetites and attention spans both welcome.

Laundry sort

  • Sorting socks by color is a real color lesson disguised as a chore. Whites here, darks there — your child is now a color sorter.
  • Mismatched socks are fine. The game is the naming, not the pairing.

Stay close, keep it playful and stop while it is still fun. There is nothing to finish here.

PRINT THE CARDS

Take the colors to the kitchen table.

All twelve color pairs print one pair to a page — the splash beside its matching picture — straight from your browser. No PDF, nothing to install.

View Printable Cards ↗

Printed cards love fridges, bedroom doors and kitchen tables. The same cards also live in the flashcards library, each with its own page.

A NOTE FROM THE PRINCIPAL

For the grown-ups.

At three, color learning is naming and noticing, not color theory: eleven color words, met one at a time in real places, do more than any worksheet. The mixing games here are previews, not tests — red + yellow = orange is worth knowing at the paint table, and nobody needs to memorize it first. Everything gives calm feedback with no scores, and the color swatches are drawn by the page itself, so the games never depend on a picture that might not load.

TIPS FOR PARENTS

How to use this class.

Sit together for the card viewing, and let your child do the tapping in the games — even when the answer looks obvious to you. Saying the color word while touching something that color is the fastest route in: “red strawberry”, “blue cup”, “yellow banana”.

Save the mixing for the very end, or for a day with paints on the table. Mixing is the reward for knowing the ingredients — and wiping up together is part of the lesson too.

Age 3 is a guide, not a deadline. If today’s class was one red thing found in the garden, today’s class was a success.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · COLORS & COLOR MIXING · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Red — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Red opens the set because it opens the mouth: it is a color children tend to shout early and often, long before quieter shades get their turn. This lesson pins the word to the feeling — loud, warm, easy to spot — and then sends your child out to find it everywhere.

    What is this?

    Red is the name for one group of things that look alike in one way: the apple, the strawberry, the stop sign and the fire engine all wear it. The splash card holds the color by itself — nothing but red — and the picture card shows it living on a real thing your child can hold and eat.

    What does it mean?

    A three-year-old does not learn red from a definition; they learn it from repetition at the moment of noticing. Every find — a tomato at lunch, a coat on the hook — files the word a little deeper. The color belongs to no single object, which is exactly why hunting for it teaches better than staring at one card.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs three things from this lesson: the word itself said clearly at the splash, at least one real twin found in your home — an apple works beautifully — and the experience of a successful hunt, because finding red things is the practice that makes the name stick. One color per day is plenty; today belongs to red.

    Why this matters

    Color words are classification practice: a child who sorts the world by red and not-red is doing the same thinking that later sorts animals, letters and shapes. Red is a friendly place to start because it is common, dramatic and easy to point at from across a room.

    What it teaches

    Visual discrimination (telling red from not-red at a distance), categorising, vocabulary, careful looking during hunts, and snack-time conversation skills when the apple twin gets eaten.

    Words to learn

    redapplesplashfindhuntsame

    Say this to your child

    ““Red! Look at this card — all red, everywhere you point. Red is the color of fire engines and strawberries. Now the other card: a shiny red apple! Red hides inside apples too. Can you spot anything red in this room? Off you go — I will count every find!””

    Step by step

    1. Hold up the splash card and say red slowly, twice — the color fills the whole card, so there is nothing else to look at and no way to miss it.
    2. Move to the picture card: a shiny red apple wearing its green leaf. Say red again at the apple — the word now belongs to something real.
    3. Hunt the room together: find five red things and touch each one as you say the word. A book cover, a mitten, a toy car all count.
    4. Snack-time finish: if you have an apple, hold it beside the picture card, name it once more, then eat your find together.
    5. Let your child play teacher — they hold the splash card, you point and guess. Get one wrong on purpose; being corrected is the best review there is.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the cards together: the splash card is one big red splash with the word red printed across it, and the picture card shows a shiny red apple wearing its green leaf. Ask your child where the red starts and stops on each card, and what the green leaf is busy not being.

    Ask your child

    “Which card is all red — the splash or the apple?” “Can you find something red bigger than your hand?” “Is the leaf red too, or a different color?” “What red thing would you like to eat?”

    What your child can say or do

    Your child might shout “red!” at everything vaguely warm-colored, march a toy fire engine around while announcing its color, or line up every red thing they own on the sofa — a correct piece of sorting work, loudly done.

    Out in the real world

    Red keeps arriving all day: strawberries at snack, a red door on the walk, the red car that passes the window. Each discovery your child announces is one more rehearsal of the word, and rehearsals — not lessons — are what make color names permanent.

    Try it together

    Red relay: scatter a few red toys and a few not-red ones, call “go red!”, and let your child fetch every red thing to the splash card as fast as legs allow. Wrong fetches are welcome too — sorting out the misses is where the learning actually happens.

    Understanding check

    Ask: “Show me red. Where is the red apple? Find me one more red thing.” The right card pointed at, the apple named and one fresh find brought back — that is the color landed.

    Parent tips

    If your child calls orange things red, do not correct flatly — set the two cards side by side and ask “same or different?” The comparison teaches the boundary more gently than a no ever could, and red keeps its good mood.

    This lesson pairs with the Red flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & Color Mixing (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · COLORS & COLOR MIXING · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Blue — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Blue gets a whole day because it fills the sky, and the sky is the biggest picture your child looks at. This lesson teaches the word at the splash, anchors it to a little blue car, then lifts everyone’s eyes upward — because blue is the rare color that arrives above your head for free, every single morning.

    What is this?

    Blue is the name for the color shared by the sky, the sea and thousands of small things: this card’s car, jeans, a blueberry, a wheelie bin. The splash card holds the color alone, the picture card shows it riding on something real, and your street supplies the rest.

    What does it mean?

    Blue teaches a quiet, powerful idea: one word can cover things of very different sizes — a car and the whole sky. A three-year-old who accepts that is doing real categorising: the word travels with the color, not with the object. That is abstraction in training wheels, and it deserves celebrating when it clicks.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs to hear blue said clearly at the splash, find at least one real blue twin nearby, and experience a spotting walk where blue things get counted out loud. Shade-words like navy and sky-blue can wait years — at three and four, everything blue is simply blue, and that is exactly right.

    Why this matters

    Blue-spotting trains distance vision and careful looking: much of the world’s blue sits far away, at the top of the view. A child practising “look up, look far” is building the same attention that later finds a friend in a playground and a letter inside a word.

    What it teaches

    Colour categorising, distance observation (sky, roofs, far cars), counting during spotting games, and the patience that comes from watching for something that is not always there — the sky is not blue every day, and noticing that is science.

    Words to learn

    bluecarskyspotlookmatch

    Say this to your child

    ““Blue! The whole card is blue — top to bottom. And here is a little blue car, beep beep! Blue rides in cars, it hides in blueberries, and sometimes the whole sky wears it. Let us count blue cars on our walk — ready? Eyes up, spotters!””

    Step by step

    1. Show the splash card and say blue twice — the whole card is one wash of it, so the word has nothing to compete with.
    2. Turn to the picture card: a little blue car with the word blue. Say the word at the car, then beep the horn together — silly, and it sticks.
    3. Hunt the house for blue: a sock, a book, a toy, the tube of toothpaste. Touch each find and say the word as you go.
    4. Take the hunt outside and count blue cars as they pass — one sighting is a win, and a whole queue of them is a parade.
    5. Finish by looking straight up: on a clear day the biggest blue thing of all is overhead, and your child gets to name it.

    Look closer at the picture

    Compare the two cards: the splash card is one big wash of blue with the word blue on it, and the picture card shows a little blue car wearing the same word. Ask your child whether any of the splash’s blue also sits on the car, and what color the wheels are not.

    Ask your child

    “Which is bigger — the blue car or the blue sky?” “Can you find two blue things that are not the same shape?” “Is your cup blue today?” “What would happen if the sky turned green?”

    What your child can say or do

    Your child might beep at every passing car, announce “blue sky!” before breakfast, or point at your jeans with great pride — naming blue on things you are wearing is a very good sign that the word has left the card and moved into the world.

    Out in the real world

    Blue turns up more than most colors once you hunt it: the car park, the letter box, a neighbor’s door, the recycling bin. Name the finds as they happen and the word rehearses itself — no lesson required, only eyes up and out.

    Try it together

    Blue treasure plate: at tidy-up time, your child collects every blue thing they can find onto one plate and presents it to you for counting. The collection is the trophy; the counting is a numbers lesson sneaking in behind the colors.

    Understanding check

    Ask: “Show me blue. Where is the little car? Find one blue thing above your head.” The right card, the car named and a ceiling, roof or sky pointed at — that is the color landed.

    Parent tips

    If your child insists the green grass is blue, swap roles — you be the confused one and ask which card the grass matches. Sorting the two splashes themselves beats being told, and the grass keeps its dignity.

    This lesson pairs with the Blue flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & Color Mixing (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · COLORS & COLOR MIXING · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Yellow — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Yellow is the color children meet with their whole face: it squints, it beams, it makes them announce things. This lesson teaches the word at the splash card, lands it on the smiling sun of the picture card, and then takes it outdoors, where dandelions and buttercups hand out free yellow finds at toddler height.

    What is this?

    Yellow is the name for the brightest common color: the sun, bananas, ducklings, egg yolks, school buses and this card’s smiling sun. The splash card shows yellow alone — the loudest card in the set — and the picture card shows it as the biggest yellow thing your child will ever see.

    What does it mean?

    Yellow arrives with weather attached: sunny days make yellow spots, grey days hide them. A child who learns yellow while watching for the sun is also learning to read the day — color words at this age are quietly weather words, mood words, morning words. The vocabulary travels with the feeling.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs the word said boldly at the splash, one glowing twin found nearby — a banana at breakfast is perfect — and one outdoor yellow hunt, because yellow is a color that waits outdoors in plain sight: flowers, autumn leaves, the paint on playground railings. Bright finds for bright eyes.

    Why this matters

    Yellow is the highest-contrast color against most backgrounds, which makes it the easiest to spot from far away and the best one for building distance-vocabulary. Early spotters of far yellow things are doing the visual groundwork that reading across a page will ask for later.

    What it teaches

    Visual discrimination at distance, brightness awareness, word-announcement confidence (yellow gets said loudly, which is speaking practice), and the beginnings of weather-talk that grows into real conversation about the day.

    Words to learn

    yellowsunbrightshinefindwarm

    Say this to your child

    ““Yellow! The brightest card we have — look how it glows! And here comes the sun, big and smiling and yellow. Can you make a sun with your arms? There it is! Yellow is in bananas and ducks and flowers. Let us find some outside — spotters ready!””

    Step by step

    1. Hold the splash card up high and say yellow loudly — a bright color deserves a bright voice, and the drama helps the word land.
    2. Move to the picture card: a big smiling yellow sun. Make a sun with your arms as you say the word again.
    3. Breakfast twin: if there is a banana, hold it next to the sun card and name them both yellow — one yellow you eat, one you cannot.
    4. Walk-hunt: count dandelions, buttercups, yellow doors and passing ducks. Yellow at child height is everywhere once the hunt starts.
    5. Close with the arms-sun again and let your child say the word as the “sun” rises above their head.

    Look closer at the picture

    Study both cards: the splash card is one big yellow splash with the word yellow on it, and the picture card shows a big smiling yellow sun with the word too. Ask your child whether the sun looks happy, and whether the splash has a face at all.

    Ask your child

    “Which card is brighter — yellow or blue?” “Can you find something yellow you could eat?” “Is the sun out today — what color does that make the day?” “What else might wear yellow?”

    What your child can say or do

    Your child might beam a huge smile at the sun card, stretch both arms into a sun-shape at random moments, or shout “yellow!” at every dandelion on the pavement — a color said with that much joy has already been learned.

    Out in the real world

    Yellow shows up at exactly child height: dandelions, fallen leaves, the yellow line at the crossing, rubber ducks at bath. Naming them turns ordinary walks into lessons nobody scheduled — the best kind.

    Try it together

    Sunrise, sunset: your child crouches small while you say “night night”, then rises slowly with arms spreading as you say “yellow morning!” — repeat with growing speed. The game is pure drama, and the color word sits right at the top of every sunrise.

    Understanding check

    Ask: “Show me yellow. Where is the sun on the cards? Find something yellow near you.” The splash named, the sun found and one fresh yellow twin pointed out — that is the color landed.

    Parent tips

    If your child calls every bright thing yellow, enjoy the phase — bright equals yellow is a correct first draft. Offer the green card next to it and ask “which one is the sun’s color?” The question sorts it out without a single correction.

    This lesson pairs with the Yellow flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & Color Mixing (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · COLORS & COLOR MIXING · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Green — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Green is the color of the outdoors doing its job: grass, leaves, bushes, the weeds in the pavement cracks. The word gets learned at the splash, planted on the big leaf of the picture card, and then taken outdoors — because green is the one color your child can literally roll around in.

    What is this?

    Green is the name for the color most plants wear: grass, leaves, peas, broccoli, beans and the leaf on this card. The splash card shows green by itself; the picture card shows one big leaf wearing it. Everything that grows tends towards green, which makes this the easiest color to find in the whole world.

    What does it mean?

    Green quietly teaches where food and plants come from: the word keeps company with growing things. A child who links green to gardens, parks and vegetables is building a first science idea — plants are green, and green means alive and growing. That idea will feed real knowledge later, one leaf at a time.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs the word at the splash, one real green twin held in the hand — a leaf, a sprig of grass — and a proper outdoor hunt. Dark green and light green both count as green at this age; if your child asks why the grass and the broccoli do not match, enjoy the question rather than answering it fully.

    Why this matters

    Green-hunting trains observation in a busy field: nature is full of greens that differ slightly, and telling leaf-green from grass-green from moss-green is fine visual discrimination — the same careful looking that later separates b from d on a page.

    What it teaches

    Nature observation, fine discrimination between similar shades, outdoor gross-motor play (stomping, rolling, crouching to find), and early science vocabulary: leaf, grass, grow, plant.

    Words to learn

    greenleafgrassgrowhuntoutside

    Say this to your child

    ““Green! Like grass and like leaves. The whole card is green — and look, the other card has one big leaf wearing it. Everything that grows is green: grass, bushes, peas. Let us go find five green things outside — touch each one and say the word with me!””

    Step by step

    1. Show the splash card and say green — then ask your child to guess what in the whole world is green before you show the next card.
    2. Reveal the picture card: one big green leaf. Lay a real leaf or a pinch of grass beside it and say the word over both.
    3. Indoor hunt: find three green things in the house — a towel, a toy, a broccoli floret if dinner is close.
    4. Outdoor hunt: five green finds, touched, named and left where they grow. Leaves, grass, bushes and weeds all count.
    5. Finish with a full-body green moment: march with big grass-stomping steps, or roll down a hill if one is nearby — green practice with the whole body.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the two cards: the splash card is one big green splash with the word green on it, and the picture card shows one big leaf with the word too. Ask your child what runs down the middle of the leaf, and whether the splash has one.

    Ask your child

    “Which is greener — the grass or the leaf card?” “Can you find a green thing taller than you?” “Does broccoli wear green too?” “What color are you wearing today — any green?”

    What your child can say or do

    Your child might crouch over pavement weeds like a scientist, bring you a bouquet of grass, or declare the park “all green, everywhere” — an accurate survey, enthusiastically delivered.

    Out in the real world

    Green dominates the outdoors: lawns, hedges, trees, the allotment, the salad at dinner. Every walk rehearses it for free — and the vegetables at dinner keep the word on the menu, where broccoli has been waiting for its moment.

    Try it together

    Green collect-and-sort: on the way home, gather a few fallen green leaves in a pocket, then sort them at the table by size — biggest to smallest. The color names the collection; the sorting does the quiet maths.

    Understanding check

    Ask: “Show me green. Where is the leaf? Find something green outside the window.” The splash named, the leaf found and one growing thing spotted — that is the color landed.

    Parent tips

    Brown autumn leaves confuse green-lovers. Say it plainly: leaves are green while they are growing and busy, and other colors when they rest. It is a first life-cycle lesson wearing a color question, and children accept it easily.

    This lesson pairs with the Green flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & Color Mixing (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · COLORS & COLOR MIXING · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Orange — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Orange is the only color that shares its name with a food, which makes this lesson nearly effortless: put a real orange in your child’s hands and the word proves itself. This lesson pairs the splash and the fruit card, then peels its way through snack time, naming the color at every stage.

    What is this?

    Orange is the name for the color between red and yellow: carrots, pumpkins, fire, traffic cones, tiger fur and this card’s round fruit. The splash card shows the pure color; the picture card shows a round orange with a green leaf — the very thing the color was named after.

    What does it mean?

    Orange demonstrates where words come from: the fruit existed first, and the color borrowed its name. A three-year-old does not need that history, but they feel its effect — saying “orange” while holding an orange is word-learning with the props included, and props make vocabulary stick.

    What does the child need to know?

    What your child needs from this lesson: the word at the splash, a real orange twin — the fruit itself, unpeeled — and the experience of naming the color while it is being peeled and eaten. Also worth tucking away: red paint mixed with yellow paint makes orange, which is the mixing game waiting later in this class.

    Why this matters

    Naming a color you are simultaneously peeling, smelling and eating is multi-sense learning — sight, smell, touch and taste all carrying one word. Lessons that load more senses load more memory, and orange is the set’s best opportunity for it.

    What it teaches

    Multi-sensory learning (color plus smell plus taste), fine motor work peeling and pulling segments, mixing-colour knowledge for later art, and the naming confidence that comes from holding the proof in your own hand.

    Words to learn

    orangefruitpeelroundnamesame

    Say this to your child

    ““Orange! The fruit that named its own color. Feel how round it is. Now we peel it... more orange! Every piece is orange. Can you say it with a mouthful? Or-ange!””

    Step by step

    1. Show the splash card and say orange — then hold a real orange next to it and let your child check that the colors match.
    2. Turn to the picture card: a round orange fruit with a green leaf. Say the word once at the card and once at the real fruit.
    3. Peel it together, slowly, naming the color as each strip comes off: orange peel, orange fruit, orange fingers afterwards.
    4. Share the segments out and count them before they disappear — orange is the snack that teaches while it feeds.
    5. End with the mixing secret: red stirred into yellow turns orange — an experiment for craft time later this week.

    Look closer at the picture

    Set the cards side by side: the splash card is one big orange splash with the word orange on it, and the picture card shows a round orange fruit with a green leaf. Ask your child which card the real fruit matches, and what the leaf on the fruit card is not.

    Ask your child

    “Is the peel a different orange than the inside?” “What else is orange — can you find two things?” “What happens when red and yellow mix?” “Is a carrot orange all the way through?”

    What your child can say or do

    Your child might hold the fruit against the splash card to prove the match, chant “orange, orange, orange” while peeling, or narrate their orange fingers — all of it is the word attaching itself to the evidence.

    Out in the real world

    Orange shows up loud and useful: traffic cones, carrots at dinner, the post van, tigers in books. Each find keeps the word warm between lessons, and the fruit bowl keeps a twin permanently in stock.

    Try it together

    Orange-and-friend sorting: set out a bowl of mixed snack pieces — orange segments, apple slices, banana rounds — and let your child sort the orange from the not-orange. Sorting food by color is a game children can eat at the end, which is excellent for morale.

    Understanding check

    Ask: “Show me orange. Which fruit is orange? What two paints make it?” The splash named, the fruit matched and the mixing secret half-remembered — that is the color landed.

    Parent tips

    If your child mixes paints and gets a muddy brown instead of orange, blame the amounts, not the idea: more yellow, a careful drop of red, and try again. Mixing is chemistry, and early failed batches are how chemists learn.

    This lesson pairs with the Orange flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & Color Mixing (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · COLORS & COLOR MIXING · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Purple — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Purple is the set’s treasure: it does not loiter on every street like red or green, so when it turns up, it turns up special. The word arrives at the splash, settles on the five-petal flower of the picture card, and then turns your home into a treasure island where one genuine find is a triumph.

    What is this?

    Purple is the name for the deep color between red and blue: grapes, plums, blackberries, lavender and the flower on this card. The splash card shows the color alone; the picture card shows a flower with five purple petals and the word too. Rarity is the lesson’s engine — scarce things get hunted harder.

    What does it mean?

    Scarcity changes how children learn a word: purple cannot be drilled by pointing at the sofa, so the word arrives through careful searching and genuine discovery. A child who has worked to find one purple thing owns that word differently — found treasure is remembered treasure.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs the word at the splash, one flower-shaped twin, and an honest treasure hunt — with pictures and books admitted as hunting grounds, because real purple is genuinely scarce. One true find in a day is a complete success; say so loudly. Also save this card: purple is the mixing challenge later — red and blue.

    Why this matters

    Rare-category learning is a different skill from common-category learning: it requires patience, sustained search and the ability to hold a target in mind while scanning. Those are attention skills wearing a color costume, and they transfer everywhere.

    What it teaches

    Sustained visual search, holding a mental target, book-and-picture scanning, patience with delayed finds, and the delight of rare discovery — which is motivation training as much as color training.

    Words to learn

    purpleflowerpetalrarefindtreasure

    Say this to your child

    ““Purple! A fancy word for a fancy color. Pur-ple — can you say it? Look at the splash, and look at the flower with its five petals. Purple is rare — it does not come out for just anyone. Let us hunt: any purple thing today is treasure!””

    Step by step

    1. Show the splash card and say purple slowly — it is a fancy word, and your child may need a couple of tries at pur-ple.
    2. Move to the picture card: a flower with five purple petals. Count the petals together, then say the color once more.
    3. Indoor treasure hunt: search the house for anything purple — a toy, a sock, a book cover. Keep expectations honest; purple hides.
    4. Open a favorite picture book and hunt purple there instead — grapes, flowers, clothing. Illustrations are a fair hunting ground.
    5. Celebrate whatever the day produced: one true purple find is a triumph, and saying so makes the word memorable.

    Look closer at the picture

    Examine both cards: the splash card is one big purple splash with the word purple on it, and the picture card shows a flower with five purple petals and the word too. Ask your child to count the petals and say whether the splash has any petals at all.

    Ask your child

    “Can you find something purple in this room?” “What purple things do we eat?” “Which is rarer here — red things or purple things?” “What two paints might make purple?”

    What your child can say or do

    Your child might whisper “purple” like a secret, present one grape as a crown jewel, or declare the hunt over after five seconds of searching — honest findings all, and the rarity is genuinely the point.

    Out in the real world

    Purple waits in specific places: grape bunches at the shop, plum skins, lavender bushes in summer, a neighbor’s purple door. Because it is rare, each real find gets remembered — and remembered words are the ones that stay.

    Try it together

    Purple ledger: keep a running family count of purple finds for a week — drawings, spots, socks, flowers — written on the fridge. A slow-growing number teaches patience with rare things, and the fridge becomes the color’s scoreboard.

    Understanding check

    Ask: “Show me purple. How many petals does the flower have? Did we find any purple treasure today?” The splash named, the petals counted and the day’s find reported — that is the color landed.

    Parent tips

    If the hunt comes up empty, plant a find: a purple bottle top on the table “discovered” later counts fully. The joy is real even when the search was helped, and the word gets its repetition either way.

    This lesson pairs with the Purple flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & Color Mixing (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · COLORS & COLOR MIXING · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Pink — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Pink usually arrives early in a child’s life — on clothes, cakes, pigs in picture books — and this lesson gives the familiar color its proper name. The splash card holds the pure color, the picture card shows a five-petal pink flower, and the house supplies the rest for a game of pink spy.

    What is this?

    Pink is the name for red’s pale cousin: piglets, bubblegum, ballet shoes, strawberry milk and this card’s flower. The splash card shows pink by itself; the picture card shows a five-petal pink flower wearing it. Pink is red with white mixed in — the first color-mixing fact many children ever learn.

    What does it mean?

    Pink teaches a quiet mixing idea: colors can be made lighter and softer, and the softened version earns its own name. A child who grasps that red-plus-white makes pink has started understanding that colors are ingredients — a thought that will run through every paint set they ever own.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs the word at the splash, one flowery twin, and a round of pink spy with a sock, a toy and a book cover standing in as the quarry. If pink is scarce at your house, clothes drawers and book covers are the richest hunting grounds — and red paint plus a spoonful of white is the mixing experiment to schedule.

    Why this matters

    I-spy games ask a child to hold one property in mind — color, not shape, not size — while scanning a roomful of competing information. That selective attention is a foundation skill for listening, reading and finding lost shoes, and pink spy is its friendliest practice run.

    What it teaches

    Selective attention during scanning, color-mixing concepts, vocabulary softness (light, pale, soft as pink-words), turn-taking when the spy roles swap, and description skills as your child explains their finds.

    Words to learn

    pinkflowersoftlightspyfind

    Say this to your child

    ““Pink! Red’s softer cousin — light and gentle, like bubblegum. Look at the splash, and look at the flower: five soft pink petals. Pink is hiding in this room right now — three somebodies. I spy something pink... can your eyes find it?””

    Step by step

    1. Show the splash card and say pink — then next to it, if you have them, show something red and let your child see how they are cousins.
    2. Turn to the picture card: a five-petal pink flower. Count the petals, say the word, and blow the flower a kiss — pink invites softness.
    3. Set out three pink things in the room before the game: a sock, a toy, a book cover — anything pink will serve.
    4. Play the pink spy round: call out “I spy with my little eye... something pink!” and let your child hunt down all three, then swap seats and take the finder’s chair yourself.
    5. End with the mixing recipe: a big blob of red, a small dot of white, stirred pale — pink is red that caught a cloud. Book the experiment for craft time this week.

    Look closer at the picture

    Hold the two cards up together: the splash card is one big pink splash with the word pink on it, and the picture card shows a five-petal pink flower with its word printed beneath. Ask your child whether all five petals are the same pink, and what sits in the spaces between them.

    Ask your child

    “Is pink closer to red or to white?” “What pink things can you eat?” “Who in the family is wearing pink today?” “What would make red softer?”

    What your child can say or do

    Your child might whisper-spy their finds, arrange pink things into a soft little pile, or ask for “the pink paint” by name at craft time — a color requested by name is a color fully owned.

    Out in the real world

    Pink lives at child level: plasters, yoghurt pots, birthday cards, the neighbour’s roses. Naming finds keeps the word in circulation, and the mixing experiment gives it a party trick at the craft table.

    Try it together

    Role-swap spy: your child hides three pink things while you cover your eyes, then spies at YOU. Being the seeker is as instructive as being the hider, and the giggle at your wrong guesses is pure learning fuel.

    Understanding check

    Ask: “Show me pink. How many petals on the flower? What do we mix with red to make it?” The splash named, the petals counted and “white” delivered — that is the color landed.

    Parent tips

    Some children rescue every pink crayon from the box and defend it fiercely. Let them — favoritism is attention, and attention is the whole engine of this lesson. The other colors will get their days.

    This lesson pairs with the Pink flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & Color Mixing (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · COLORS & COLOR MIXING · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Brown — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Brown is the homeliest color in the set and the one that comes with cuddles attached: teddies, dogs, chocolate, bread crusts, the garden shed. The lesson starts at the splash, moves to the smiling teddy on the picture card, then sends your child off to introduce their own brownest friend formally.

    What is this?

    Brown is the name for the earthy color of tree trunks, soil, teddy bears, dogs and chocolate. The splash card shows brown by itself; the picture card shows a smiling brown teddy bear. And when many paints meet in one pot, brown is what they become — a fact worth announcing the day the paint all swirls together.

    What does it mean?

    Brown is comfort’s color: the toys children sleep with, the animals they trust, the snacks they beg for. Learning the word attaches language to already-loved things, which is the easiest kind of vocabulary there is — the feeling arrives first, and the word just moves in.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs the word at the splash, one bear-shaped twin, and a completed introduction to their own brownest toy or pet. Save the mixing fact too: many colors stirred together make brown, so the day all the paints merge is chemistry, not a disaster — a reframe that has rescued many craft afternoons.

    Why this matters

    Emotionally warm words are learned faster and kept longer: brown rides on love of teddies and chocolate, so its repetitions are welcome ones. A child who names their own bear “brown bear” is doing exactly the right thing — beloved objects are the best vocabulary anchors a house contains.

    What it teaches

    Emotionally anchored vocabulary, tactile exploration (fur, wood, bark, soil), care-taking talk when the teddy gets introduced, and mixing knowledge that turns paint accidents into science.

    Words to learn

    brownteddybearhugsoftfind

    Say this to your child

    ““Brown! The cuddle color. Look at the splash — all brown. And here is a teddy bear, smiling and brown and soft. Have you got a brown friend at home? Go and get them — we will introduce them to the card, brown bear to brown bear!””

    Step by step

    1. Show the splash card and say brown — then ask your child who in the house is brown, and enjoy the answers before showing any more cards.
    2. Turn to the picture card: a smiling brown teddy bear. Say the word at the bear, then give the card a hug — brown is a hugging color.
    3. Formal introduction: fetch your child’s own brown teddy, dog or wooden toy, stand it beside the card and introduce them by name and color.
    4. Brown snack hunt: bread crusts, a chocolate square, a biscuit — name each one brown before it is eaten.
    5. Close with the mixing fact: when many paint colors swirl together, brown is what they make — chemistry wearing a cuddly coat.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at both cards: the splash card is one big brown splash with the word brown on it, and the picture card shows a smiling brown teddy bear with the word too. Ask your child what the bear’s face is doing, and where its brown parts stop.

    Ask your child

    “Is your teddy the same brown as the card?” “What brown things can we eat?” “What lives in the brown soil?” “What happens when all the paints mix together?”

    What your child can say or do

    Your child might introduce their teddy with a handshake, demand chocolate “because it is brown, that is its color”, or hug the card — the vocabulary has landed when the logic arrives, and this logic is adorable and correct.

    Out in the real world

    Brown is steady company: the dog across the street, tree trunks at the park, the garden soil, the crusts at lunch. Because brown things are usually touchable, this word collects more hands-on repetition than most — fur, bark and crusts are all fair samples.

    Try it together

    Bear’s picnic: lay a cloth, seat the brownest toys around it, and serve brown snacks — bread, biscuits, chocolate. Name every brown item as it is served. The color word becomes the picnic’s language, and tidy-up eats the evidence.

    Understanding check

    Ask: “Show me brown. Who is your brownest friend? What do many mixed paints make?” Splash answered, friend introduced and “brown” delivered — that is the color landed.

    Parent tips

    If your child grieves that their teddy is “only brown”, flip it: brown is the color of teddies, dogs and chocolate — objectively the best company of any color in the set. The bear’s status will recover immediately.

    This lesson pairs with the Brown flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & Color Mixing (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · COLORS & COLOR MIXING · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Black — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Black is the set’s drama: night skies, big boots, pandas, and the handsome cat on this card. Children often take to black for the theatre of it — cats, boots, the night sky — and the lesson uses that — teach the word at the splash, land it on the cat with the yellow eyes, then run a quick hunt where black’s high contrast makes finds almost instant.

    What is this?

    Black is the name for the darkest color: night, tires, shadows, pandas, spider legs and this card’s cat. The splash card shows black by itself; the picture card shows a black cat with yellow eyes — the yellow a helpful reminder that black things often come with something bright nearby.

    What does it mean?

    Black teaches contrast without saying so: the cat’s yellow eyes, stars on a night sky, chalk on a board — black is the background that makes other colors shout. A child who notices that black makes bright things brighter is doing real perception work, dressed as cat appreciation.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs the word at the splash, one cat-shaped twin, and one quick hunt with an easy win — black is common enough on shoes and books that three finds take a minute. Share the mixing secret too: many paints mixed make brown rather than black, and true black comes from a tube — a fact children test and never forget.

    Why this matters

    Black’s high contrast trains visual search: finds are fast, so a hunt delivers many successes in a short session. Fast successes keep a three-year-old hunting, and hunting — not sitting — is how color words get learned at this age.

    What it teaches

    Contrast perception, visual search with quick rewards, night-and-day vocabulary as black connects to bedtime, and the mixing knowledge that separates accidental brown from true black.

    Words to learn

    blackcatnightdarkspoteyes

    Say this to your child

    ““Black! The darkest, most dramatic color — like night and like this cat. Look at the card: black fur, and those bright yellow eyes! Black makes bright things pop. Quick — three black things in this room, sixty seconds, go!””

    Step by step

    1. Show the splash card and say black — then ask what else in the whole world is black, and gather the night, the tires and the boots.
    2. Turn to the picture card: a black cat with yellow eyes. Say the word at the cat, then whisper it like a secret — black is a whispering color.
    3. Quick indoor hunt: three black things in sixty seconds — shoes, a chair, the telly. The speed is the fun; black finds fast.
    4. Read the eyes: point at the cat’s yellow eyes and say how the bright eyes show up best on black — contrast, demonstrated by a cat.
    5. Close with the mixing secret: stir every paint together and brown appears, not black — true black only comes from a tube, and children who test it never forget it.

    Look closer at the picture

    Study both cards: the splash card is one big black splash with the word black on it, and the picture card shows a black cat with yellow eyes and the word too. Ask your child where the eyes are looking, and what color sits inside them.

    Ask your child

    “What black things come out at night?” “Which pops more on black — yellow or black?” “Where are the panda’s black parts?” “Can you find something black you can wear?”

    What your child can say or do

    Your child might creep around like a black cat, announce bedtime as “black sky time”, or win the sixty-second hunt in ten seconds flat — black’s speed is real, and a child who exploits it has understood contrast all by themselves.

    Out in the real world

    Black is everywhere daily: tires at the crossing, the letter box, shoes by the door, bats in books. The finds come so quickly that this color easily collects its repetitions before dinner — the fastest lesson in the set to keep alive.

    Try it together

    Shadow theater: dim the lamp, shine a torch on the wall and make black hand-shadows — a bird, a dog, a spider. Black is the color of the show, and the night-sky connection gives the word a bedtime job for years.

    Understanding check

    Ask: “Show me black. What color are the cat’s eyes? What do many mixed paints make?” The splash named, the eyes reported and “brown” delivered — that is the color landed.

    Parent tips

    Some children find black slightly frightening after dark. Keep the word’s company friendly: the cat, the panda, the boots. If bedtime wobbles, add stars — black sky with stars is the color’s kindest costume.

    This lesson pairs with the Black flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & Color Mixing (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · COLORS & COLOR MIXING · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    White — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    White is the quiet one: it does not shout like red or glow like yellow, but it holds the sky’s best show — clouds. The word is learned quietly at the splash, placed on one puffy cloud, and then everyone lies down on the floor or the lawn for cloud-spotting, which is color practice disguised as daydreaming.

    What is this?

    White is the name for the palest color: clouds, milk, snow, paper, sheep and this card’s cloud. The splash card shows white by itself; the picture card shows one puffy white cloud. White is also the great lightener — mixed into any color, it makes the paler version: pink from red, sky from blue.

    What does it mean?

    White teaches the light end of color mixing: colors have pale cousins, and white is the ingredient that makes them. A child who learns that white turns red into pink holds a genuinely useful idea — the same one that later explains pale orange, pale green and every pastel they will ever mix.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs the word at the splash, one cloud-shaped twin, and one proper cloud-spotting session — lying back, finding shapes, naming them white. Shape-talk is welcome (today a bunny, tomorrow a boat) as long as the color word does the anchoring. Save the mixing fact: white plus red makes pink, and this card is the reason.

    Why this matters

    Cloud-spotting is sustained looking at slow-moving targets — the gentlest possible attention training, done flat on your back. It also builds comfort with ambiguity: clouds are never quite any shape, and accepting “sort of a bunny” is early flexible thinking.

    What it teaches

    Sustained sky-watching, shape-seeing in ambiguous forms, mixing knowledge (white lightens), bath-time vocabulary around foam and bubbles, and the calm that comes from lying still and looking up together.

    Words to learn

    whitecloudskymilklookup

    Say this to your child

    ““White! The quietest card in our set — soft like milk and like clouds. Look at the splash, and look at the puffy cloud floating on its card. What does that cloud look like to you? A bunny? A boat? Now look up — what are the real clouds doing today?””

    Step by step

    1. Show the splash card and say white quietly — it is the set’s softest color, and a soft voice suits it.
    2. Turn to the picture card: one puffy white cloud with the word white. Ask what the cloud reminds them of, and accept any answer.
    3. Milk moment: at the next drink, hold the cup up and say white — the most everyday white twin in the house.
    4. Lie back together on floor or lawn and spot real clouds: find one, name it white, then let shapes take over the conversation.
    5. Close with the mixing promise: white paint plus red paint makes pink — an experiment to run at the craft table this week.

    Look closer at the picture

    Compare the cards: the splash card is one big white splash with the word white on it, and the picture card shows one puffy white cloud with the word too. Ask your child whether the cloud fills its card the way the splash does, and what shows through around it.

    Ask your child

    “Is milk white or yellow?” “What falls white in winter?” “Can a cloud be any other color?” “What do we mix with red to make pink?”

    What your child can say or do

    Your child might point at every cloud for a week, stir milk dramatically at breakfast, or request “the white paint” to lighten everything at craft time — white invites mixing experiments, and every pastel they invent is the lesson working.

    Out in the real world

    White waits in ordinary places: milk at breakfast, foam at bath time, paper all day long, the first snow if winter sends it. The mixing trick gives the word a party piece, and the sky does the advertising for free.

    Try it together

    Shape-shift the cloud: draw or cut a big white cloud from paper, then ask what it could be today — a sheep, a dragon, a spaceship. The cloud keeps its color; the imagination gets the exercise. Both grow.

    Understanding check

    Ask: “Show me white. What is floating on the picture card? What does white make when it mixes with red?” The splash named, the cloud found and “pink” delivered — that is the color landed.

    Parent tips

    On grey days, the sky steals white’s show. Teach the honest version: clouds are white up close and greyer when heavy with rain — weather changes colors, and noticing that is real observation, not a mistake.

    This lesson pairs with the White flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & Color Mixing (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · COLORS & COLOR MIXING · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Gray — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Gray rarely wins a child’s first-favorite vote, which is exactly why it deserves a lesson: once the word arrives, pigeons, kerbstones and storm clouds all start introducing themselves. The lesson points the word at the splash, parks it on the gentle elephant, and then marches it home, because gray comes with its own walk and its own sound.

    What is this?

    Gray is the name for the in-between color of rain days: elephants, pigeons, storm clouds, cobblestones, Grandma’s coat. The splash card shows gray by itself; the picture card shows a gentle gray elephant. Gray is also black and white’s baby — mixed together, the two make it, which is a mixing fact worth saving for craft time.

    What does it mean?

    Gray carries weather: grey days used to be dull days, but once the word arrives, grey days become elephant days, pigeon days, spotting days. Naming a color changes how a child meets the weather it rides on — the same sky becomes interesting instead of cancelled.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs the word at the splash, one elephant twin, and one full elephant march — big slow steps, one arm for a trunk. Keep expectations flexible on shade: silver, charcoal and storm-gray all answer to gray at this age, and the pigeon outside is a free, self-renewing twin.

    Why this matters

    Gray-hunting works in bad weather, which makes it the set’s rainy-day insurance: pigeons and pavements deliver finds when green and yellow stay home. A color with an all-weather hunting ground keeps the lesson running every day of the year.

    What it teaches

    Shade flexibility (many grays count as gray), gross-motor imitation in the elephant march, weather vocabulary, sound play with the elephant trumpet, and observation of common urban wildlife — pigeons are underserved teachers.

    Words to learn

    grayelephantrainpigeonstompfind

    Say this to your child

    ““Gray! Like a big gentle elephant — can you stomp like one? One big gray step... and another! Gray is the color of rainy days and pigeons and this whole card. What else can you find that wears gray? The pavement counts! The pigeon counts! Everything slow and gray counts!””

    Step by step

    1. Show the splash card and say gray — then swing your arm like a trunk and let your child guess the animal before you show it.
    2. Reveal the picture card: a gentle gray elephant. Say the word again, then attempt a trumpet together — the sound is half the fun.
    3. Elephant march across the room: heavy gray steps, one swinging arm for a trunk, the word said at every stomp.
    4. Window hunt: pigeons, parked cars, the pavement, the sky — find three gray things without leaving the glass.
    5. Save the mixing fact: black paint and white paint stir into gray, and your child can mix a whole herd of slightly different elephants at craft time.

    Look closer at the picture

    Put the two cards next to each other: the splash card is one big gray splash with the word gray on it, and the picture card shows a gentle gray elephant with the word too. Ask your child what the elephant’s trunk is doing, and whether the splash has a trunk anywhere.

    Ask your child

    “Is the elephant bigger than our house?” “What gray bird visits the pavement?” “What does black paint plus white paint make?” “Is today a gray day — what does the sky say?”

    What your child can say or do

    Your child might march and trumpet at random hours, greet every pigeon by its color, or report that “today is gray, like the elephant” — a weather report and a color lesson arriving in the same breath, which is exactly the plan.

    Out in the real world

    Gray is the city’s color and the sky’s mood: kerbstones, squirrels, storm clouds, the neighbor’s car. The finds need no sunshine, which keeps this word in daily rotation — and every pigeon is a repetition with wings.

    Try it together

    Herd of elephants: mix gray paint at the table (black plus white, stirred slowly), paint one big elephant, then mix a slightly different gray and paint a smaller one beside it. A herd of subtly different grays is shade-vocabulary the children make themselves.

    Understanding check

    Ask: “Show me gray. Which animal is gray? What two paints make it?” The splash named, the elephant trumpeted and “black plus white” delivered — that is the color landed.

    Parent tips

    Do not fuss if silver, charcoal and “rain color” all get called gray — the big word comes first and the fine shades can wait years. A generous gray is a well-loved gray, and the pigeons do not mind.

    This lesson pairs with the Gray flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & Color Mixing (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · COLORS & COLOR MIXING · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Rainbow — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    The rainbow closes the set the way it closes a storm: with everything at once. This lesson is the graduation — every color your child has learned, marching together in line, in one splash and one sky.

    What is this?

    A rainbow is the arc of colors that sometimes appears in the sky when sun meets rain: red, then orange, then yellow, then green, then blue, then purple — always that exact order. The splash card shows the colors flowing together in one splash; the picture card shows a real rainbow arched across the sky. Both wear the word rainbow.

    What does it mean?

    The rainbow is color knowledge made visible as one thing: six words your child owns, joined into an arc they can now name in order. Reciting a sequence — and knowing there IS an order — is early maths wearing a sky: it is the same skill as counting, and it will not stay inside rainbows.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs all six colors named at the splash, one recitation with pointing, and one drawn rainbow — half a dozen crayons, six arcs, whatever paper is at hand. A true rainbow asks for sunshine and shower together, so the spotting is a patience game: a rainbow drawn from memory counts just as much as a find, and the sky will deliver the real thing someday, unannounced.

    Why this matters

    Sequencing is the quiet prize here: saying colors in order is ordering, and ordering is the front door to counting, alphabet and taking turns. The rainbow packages that skill in the most beautiful object in the set — which is why it goes last, when every color in it is already known.

    What it teaches

    Sequencing and order (six colors, fixed positions), recall of the whole set, drawing with intent (six arcs, chosen colors), patience for rare real-world events, and the graduation pride of finishing a whole class.

    Words to learn

    rainbowcolorsarcorderskyname

    Say this to your child

    ““A rainbow! Every color we know, all in one place. Red, then orange, then yellow, then green, then blue, then purple — say each one as I point. That is their order; rainbows always keep it. Now let us draw one — every color gets a turn, in a big arch across the paper!””

    Step by step

    1. Show the splash card and name the colors as you point: red first, then orange, yellow after that, green, blue, and purple bringing up the rear — slowly, in order.
    2. Say them again as one run, singing if you can, while your child points at each color in turn on the card.
    3. Turn to the picture card: a real rainbow arched across the sky. Ask which of the six colors your child can find on it.
    4. Draw one together: choose six crayons and lay down six arcs across whatever paper you have, naming each color as it takes its turn.
    5. Hang the drawing where the weather can be watched from, and keep the patience game open: a real rainbow is coming someday, and your child will be the first to shout.

    Look closer at the picture

    Both cards together now: the splash card is one big splash striped with every rainbow color and the word rainbow on it, and the picture card shows a real rainbow arched across the sky with the word too. Ask your child to find red on both, then blue on both — the order holds on each card.

    Ask your child

    “What comes after red in a rainbow?” “What does a rainbow need — what kind of day?” “Can you point at the top of the arc?” “Which color is your favorite today?”

    What your child can say or do

    Your child might sing the color run at random moments, check the sky after every rain shower for weeks, or correct your drawing when blue jumps the queue — an ordered sequence defended is a sequence truly learned.

    Out in the real world

    Rainbows keep a low schedule, but their colors rehearse daily: red cars, orange cones, yellow ducks, green grass, blue bins, purple flowers. The set has taught the parts; the world keeps offering the whole — and one real rainbow collects them all at once.

    Try it together

    Color-line parade: six papers or toys in rainbow order across the floor, and your child marches the arc from red to purple, naming each as they pass. Reverse it for the encore — going backwards is harder, funnier, and the real test of the sequence.

    Understanding check

    Ask: “Name the rainbow colors in order. What do we need besides rain? Show me the top of the arc.” Six colors recited, sun-plus-rain remembered and a finger at the sky — that is the whole class, landed.

    Parent tips

    If your child asks what makes a rainbow, keep it honest and small: sun shining through raindrops makes the colors stand up in an arc. The full physics can wait; the wonder cannot, so protect it and let the sky keep its trick.

    This lesson pairs with the Rainbow flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & Color Mixing (Preschool).
